Surviving a major earthquake is a massive relief, but the danger does not end when the initial shaking stops. One of the most critical aspects of
earthquake safety
is understanding and preparing for aftershocks. These subsequent tremors can cause further damage to already weakened structures and pose significant risks to your physical and emotional well-being. By following proper aftershock safety tips, you can protect yourself and your family during the tense hours, days, and even months following a significant seismic event.
What Are Aftershocks and Why Do They Happen?
Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes that occur in the same general area during the days to years following a larger event, known as the "mainshock." They represent the earth's crust adjusting to the new stress distribution caused by the mainshock's fault rupture.
Seismologists use specific scientific principles to understand these sequences. Omori's Law, formulated in 1894, states that the frequency of aftershocks decreases roughly in proportion to the time elapsed since the mainshock. Simply put, you will experience the most aftershocks immediately after the main earthquake, and they will gradually become less frequent over time.
Another key principle is Båth's Law, which observes that the largest aftershock is typically about 1.1 to 1.2 magnitudes smaller than the mainshock. So, if a magnitude 7.0 mainshock occurs, you can expect the largest aftershock to be roughly a magnitude 5.8 to 5.9. Understanding these scientific rules helps emergency planners and residents know what to expect when checking recent
earthquakes near me
.

How Long Do Aftershocks Last After an Earthquake?
One of the most common questions is how long aftershocks will last. The answer depends heavily on the size of the mainshock. A larger mainshock will produce a longer and more vigorous aftershock sequence.
In the first few hours and days, aftershocks can be nearly constant, rattling nerves and disrupting rescue efforts. Over the following weeks and months, they will decrease in both frequency and magnitude. However, for very large earthquakes (magnitude 8.0 or higher), aftershocks can continue for years or even decades.
Aftershock Safety Tips: What to Do When Shaking Resumes
Knowing
what to do during an earthquake
applies equally to aftershocks. The primary directive remains the same: Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Because buildings may have been compromised by the mainshock, it is even more critical to react swiftly to subsequent tremors.
Drop to your hands and knees immediately to prevent being knocked over.
Cover your head and neck with your arms, and crawl under a sturdy desk or table if one is nearby.
Hold on to your shelter until the shaking completely stops.
If you are in bed when an aftershock strikes, stay there and cover your head and neck with a pillow.
If you are outdoors, move to a clear area away from buildings, trees, streetlights, and power lines.

How to Assess Your Home for Damage After an Earthquake
Once the main shaking has stopped and you have navigated any immediate aftershocks, you must assess your environment for hazards. If you notice severe damage, you must evacuate immediately. Learning how to
earthquake proof your home
beforehand can minimize these issues, but inspection is always necessary.
Structural Damage Signs
Look for large cracks in walls or foundations, leaning walls, or sagging roofs. If a building looks visibly distorted, do not enter it or stay inside. Even a moderate aftershock could cause a weakened structure to collapse completely.
Utility Hazards
Gas Leaks: Smell for gas (a "rotten egg" odor) or listen for a hissing sound. If you suspect a gas leak, open a window and leave the building immediately. Turn off the main gas valve from the outside if you know how, and report it to the gas company.
Electrical Issues: Look for frayed wires, sparks, or the smell of burning insulation. If safe, turn off the electricity at the main fuse box or circuit breaker.
Water Damage: Shut off the main water valve if you suspect water lines are broken to prevent flooding and protect your clean water supply.
Emotional and Psychological Recovery After an Earthquake
The physical impacts of earthquakes are obvious, but the psychological toll can be just as severe. The constant threat of aftershocks can cause acute anxiety, stress, and sleep deprivation. It is normal to feel jumpy, hyper-vigilant, or emotionally exhausted.
Children are particularly vulnerable to trauma from ongoing tremors. Provide them with reassurance, maintain routines where possible, and encourage them to express their fears. For adults, acknowledging the stress and seeking community support can be highly beneficial. If symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) or severe anxiety persist, do not hesitate to seek professional mental health assistance.
Aftershock Preparedness: Staying Ready for the Next One
Because aftershocks are inevitable following a major earthquake, you must remain in a state of heightened preparedness. Keep your emergency supplies accessible and ensure your environment is safe.
Keep a sturdy pair of shoes and a flashlight by your bed to navigate broken glass or debris safely in the dark.
Ensure your
earthquake emergency kit
is fully stocked, easily accessible, and has a first aid kit, water, and non-perishable food.
Keep your mobile devices charged using power banks, as power grids may be unstable.
Keep pathways to exits clear of fallen furniture or debris to allow for quick evacuation if necessary.
Understanding Aftershock Sequences: Real-World Examples
History provides stark reminders of how prolonged and damaging aftershock sequences can be. By examining past events, we can better understand the reality of post-earthquake environments.
Following the devastating 2011 mainshock in
New Zealand
, the city of Christchurch experienced thousands of aftershocks over several years. Some of these aftershocks were large enough to cause additional severe damage and loss of life, completely reshaping the city's recovery timeline.
The 2023 earthquake in
Turkey
and Syria featured a massive magnitude 7.8 mainshock, followed just hours later by an unusually large magnitude 7.5 aftershock (or triggered earthquake) on an adjacent fault. This compounded the catastrophe, destroying buildings that had barely survived the initial quake and complicating rescue efforts.
Similarly, the 2024 Noto earthquake in
Japan
generated a rigorous aftershock sequence that triggered additional landslides and hindered the delivery of aid to isolated coastal communities.
When Is It Safe to Go Back Inside After an Earthquake?
Deciding when to re-enter a building is one of the most difficult choices following an earthquake. Never enter a building that has visible structural damage. In many regions, structural engineers and local authorities will inspect buildings and apply a tagging system to indicate safety.
Green Tag: The building is considered safe for occupancy, though minor damage may exist.
Yellow Tag: The building has sustained moderate damage. Access is restricted, and it may only be safe to enter briefly to retrieve essential belongings.
Red Tag: The building is severely damaged and is unsafe to enter under any circumstances.
If your home has not been officially inspected, err on the side of caution. If you have any doubts about its structural integrity, stay outside or seek a community shelter until a professional assessment can be made. Remember, your safety is far more important than your property.
